Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I. Ille Ego Oh! list to me: for I’m about To catch the fire of Chaucer, And spin in doleful measure out The tale of Johnny Raw, sir; Who, bent upon a desperate plan To make the people stare, Set off full speed for Hindoostan Upon Old Poulter’s mare. Tramp! tramp! across the land he went; Splash! splash! across the sea; And then he gave his bragging vent— “Pray who can ride like me? “For I’m the man, who sallied forth To rout the classic forces, And swore this mare was far more worth Than both fierce Hector’s horses. “Old Homer from his throne I struck, To Virgil gave a punch, And in the place of both I stuck The doughty Mother Bunch, “To France I galloped on my roan, Whose mettle nought can quail; There squatted on the tomb of Joan, And piped a dismal tale. “A wild and wondrous stave I sung, To make my hearers weep: But when I looked, and held my tongue, I found them fast asleep! “Oh! then, a furious oath I swore, Some dire revenge to seek; And conjured up, to make them roar, Stout Taffy and his leek. “To Heaven and Hell I rode away, In spite of wind and weather: Trumped up a diabolic lay; And cursed them all together. “Now, Proteus! rise, thou changeful seer! To spirit up my mare: In every shape but those appear, Which Taste and Nature wear.”

### I. Ille Ego

Hear me now, for I intend to borrow Chaucer’s flame and recount, in mournful verse, the story of Johnny Raw. Determined to amaze the public with a reckless undertaking, he raced toward Hindustan astride Old Poulter’s mare.

Over the countryside he pounded—tramp after tramp—and through the waters he plunged—splash after splash. Then he burst into boastful speech:

“Who, I ask, can equal my horsemanship? I am the champion who rode out to overthrow the armies of classical learning, declaring that this single mare surpassed both of mighty Hector’s steeds.

“I knocked ancient Homer from his seat of honor, struck Virgil with my fist, and installed the formidable Mother Bunch where those two poets had once stood.

“Mounted on my spirited roan, whose courage nothing could defeat, I galloped into France. There I perched upon Joan’s tomb and played a sorrowful story.

“I sang a strange and astonishing verse designed to bring my listeners to tears. Yet when I stopped and examined them, I discovered that every one of them had fallen sound asleep.

“Enraged, I uttered a terrible vow and resolved to take dreadful revenge. To make the crowd bellow, I summoned sturdy Taffy together with his leek.

“Defying storms and every other hardship, I rode off through both Heaven and Hell. I invented a devilish song and heaped curses upon them all at once.

“And now, Proteus, arise—ever-changing prophet! Breathe new spirit into my mare. Assume every possible form except those belonging to good Taste and faithful Nature.”
outputs.L3:
The narrator introduces a mock-heroic tale centered on Johnny Raw, an absurdly ambitious rider who mounts Old Poulter’s mare and sets off toward Hindoostan. His journey is motivated less by courage or noble purpose than by a desire to attract public attention and establish his fame. By presenting this ridiculous expedition in the elevated language of epic poetry, the narrator humorously contrasts Johnny’s grand self-image with the unimpressive reality of his undertaking.

Johnny openly boasts that both his horsemanship and his literary talents exceed those of the greatest figures of classical antiquity. In his imagination, he has outdone the legendary heroes of epic and replaced Homer and Virgil as the supreme poetic authority. These extravagant claims reveal his vanity and lack of self-awareness: rather than proving his genius, they expose the enormous gap between his pretensions and his abilities.

His travels eventually take him to France, where he visits the tomb of Joan of Arc. There, Johnny performs a sorrowful song intended to move and impress his listeners. Instead of responding with admiration or grief, however, the audience falls asleep. This comic failure undermines Johnny’s belief in his own poetic power and turns what he imagines as a scene of profound artistic triumph into one of embarrassment.

Furious at being ignored, Johnny abandons mournful sentiment and seeks revenge through increasingly extravagant compositions. His songs become wild, supernatural, and even diabolical, as though sheer noise, terror, and grotesque invention might succeed where genuine feeling has failed. The more desperately he tries to command attention, the further his art departs from restraint, judgment, and common sense.

At last, Johnny invokes Proteus, the shape-shifting god, asking him to transform and inspire Old Poulter’s mare in every conceivable form. Yet his request pointedly excludes the very forms sanctioned by taste and nature. The conclusion therefore sharpens the satire: Johnny’s pursuit of novelty and fame leads him not toward true artistic greatness, but toward deliberate distortion, excess, and absurdity. His journey becomes a parody of heroic adventure and poetic ambition, exposing the folly of writers who mistake extravagance and self-promotion for genius.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents “Johnny Raw” as an ambitious but hopelessly tasteless poet whose desire for literary fame is matched only by his inability to understand what makes poetry effective. His career is described as a mock-heroic journey: the language and structure elevate his artistic ambitions as though they were the exploits of a great epic hero, while his repeated failures reveal how trivial and misguided those ambitions really are. Instead of studying the classical masters or learning from established models of beauty, proportion, and judgment, Johnny dismisses them as stale and conventional. He believes that originality consists simply in avoiding whatever earlier poets valued.

In search of novelty, Johnny turns toward increasingly strange, violent, and grotesque subjects. He assumes that shocking images, exaggerated emotions, and sensational incidents will automatically produce powerful verse. Yet each new attempt demonstrates the opposite. His poems substitute noise for energy, ugliness for sublimity, and obscurity for depth. Although he wants to astonish his readers, he succeeds only in boring, confusing, or repelling them. The more desperately he pursues originality, the further he moves from genuine imagination and human feeling.

The mock-heroic treatment sharpens the satire by contrasting Johnny’s grand view of himself with the poor quality of his achievements. He behaves like a daring innovator venturing into unexplored territory, but his supposed discoveries are merely displays of bad taste. His inflated style cannot conceal the emptiness of his ideas, and his contempt for artistic discipline leaves him without the technical skill needed to transform unusual material into convincing poetry. Even potentially dramatic subjects become ridiculous in his hands because he lacks restraint, judgment, and sensitivity to nature.

Johnny’s failed career therefore serves as a broader criticism of poets who mistake novelty for genius. The poem does not argue that poetry must merely imitate the past or avoid difficult subjects. Rather, it insists that innovation must be guided by taste, knowledge, and genuine poetic ability. Classical learning provides standards against which ambition can be disciplined, while attention to nature and authentic emotion gives poetry substance. Without these qualities, originality becomes eccentricity and grandeur collapses into bombast.

Ultimately, the audience’s rejection of Johnny’s work exposes the gap between his self-importance and his actual talent. He longs to be admired as a bold poetic genius, but his efforts produce neither pleasure nor insight. Through his increasingly absurd search for sensational material, the poem shows that shock alone cannot sustain art. Lasting poetry requires more than ambition and extravagant language: it depends on judgment, craft, natural feeling, and an understanding of what truly moves the reader.

### *Ille* and *Ego* in Chaucer

The Latin words *ille* (“that man” or “he”) and *ego* (“I”) express two contrasting ways of presenting identity: from the outside and from within. Their combination recalls the classical formula *ille ego*—“I am that man”—most famously associated with the traditional opening attributed to Virgil: *Ille ego qui quondam…* (“I am he who once…”). The phrase connects a public literary figure, “that man,” with the speaking authorial “I.”

This tension is central to Geoffrey Chaucer’s poetry. Chaucer frequently inserts a version of himself into his works, but his poetic *ego* is rarely identical to the historical author. In *The House of Fame*, the dreamer is called “Geffrey,” yet he appears uncertain, passive, and overwhelmed by the confusing world of fame. Likewise, in *The Canterbury Tales*, “Chaucer” is both the supposed recorder of the pilgrimage and one of its fictional participants. The other pilgrims even judge his appearance and interrupt his tale. Thus, the author becomes *ille*: a figure observed and described by others.

At the same time, Chaucer’s narrators repeatedly use *ego*, speaking in the first person and claiming direct experience: “I saw,” “I heard,” or “I will tell.” Such claims seem to promise authority, but Chaucer often undermines them through irony. His narrators forget details, misunderstand events, or insist that they are merely reporting what others have said. The first-person voice therefore does not guarantee a stable or truthful identity.

The relationship between *ille* and *ego* helps explain Chaucer’s distinctive self-presentation. He is simultaneously the speaking “I” and “that Chaucer” transformed into a literary character. By moving between these positions, Chaucer draws attention to the gap between author, narrator, and textual persona. His poetry suggests that identity—like storytelling itself—is shaped by perspective: the person who says “I” can always become “he,” a figure interpreted by others.
